description.narrative: The development objective of the Expanding Rural Finance Project for Mexico is to expand the availability of finance to the rural economy. The project comprises of two components. The first component, expanding credit for rural micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) consists of following two sub-components: (i) credit line through participating financial intermediary (PFIs) to MSMEs; and (ii) supporting rural financial development agency (FND) pilots for rural finance. The second component, strengthening institutional capacity for sustainable rural finance consists of following two sub-components: (i) modernization of banking systems; and (ii) strengthening rural financial institutions.
The project's development objective is to expand the availability of finance to the rural economy.

title.narrative: Average non-performing loans ratio for PFIs receiving project funds

comment.narrative:
<p>???????The target of this indicator was achieved. </p>
<p>During implementation, 255 participating financial intermediaries (PFIs), that complied with the eligibility criteria of the Project, channeled subloans in rural areas without compromising the quality of their loan portfolios. Repayment by the final borrowers was appropriate as evidenced by low levels of non-performing loans (NPLs) during the life of the Project, which was below the 6 percent established as target for this indicator. Ofthe 255 PFIs, 89 percent were unsupervised by financial regulators and either registered as SOFOMES (42 percent) or as producer associations, which FND refers to as dispersoras (47 percent). FND has been successful in working with this type of financial intermediaries that have built the capacity of knowing their clients/members in rural areas which  has contributed to improve their credit analysis process, thus, improve their levels of NPLs.    </p>

title.narrative: Percentage of FND branch offices using the new core banking system.

comment.narrative: <p>FND has been able to implement the improvements in its IT system and its core banking in all its branches and now it is able to advance in its strategy of improving the user experience by facilitating online services including the use of mobile applications (iOS and Android) for internal and external clients. In addition, the last CBNV supervision report (end of 2019) has not identified the need to make any corrective actions directly linked to the IT and core banking of FND.</p>

title.narrative: Number of final beneficiaries with loans financed with project funds (cumulative)

comment.narrative:
<p>FND channeled subloan with Project funds to 139,253 final borrowers. The average loan size was US$1,850 (about MXN 35,728) below the original loan size estimate of US$5,000. The main reason the Project exceeded its original target is due to the number of final borrowers that applied to get access to microcredit (below US$1,000), 84 percent of final borrowers were microfinance beneficiaries, 83 percent of credit recipients were women,12.9 percent of final borrowers lived in highlymarginalized and marginalized municipalities. If considered at the community level instead of the municipal level, 22 percent of final borrowers were located in communities classified as marginalized or highly marginalized by the National Council for Population (CONAPO), and 12.3 percent were first-time borrowers from formal financial institutions.</p>

<p>Moreover, FND using their own funds, disbursed 150,043 additional subloans applying the same eligibility criteria defined for this Project; Eighty-four of final borrowers were microfinance beneficiaries, 76 percent of credit recipients were women, 20.6 percent were located in communities classified as marginalized or highly marginalized, and 23.5 percent were first-time borrowers from formal financial institutions.</p>

<p> </p>

title.narrative: Number of loans disbursed under project (cumulative)

comment.narrative:
<p>With the Project support, 173,981 subloans for productive purposes were disbursed with Project funds to 139,253 MSMEs in rural areas. The average loan size was US$1,850 (about MXN35,728), below the original average loan size estimate of US$ 5,000. The main reason the Project exceeded its original target is due to the number of final borrowers that applied to get access to a microcredit (below US$ 1,000). Microcredit represented 80 percent of the total number of subloans. The Project disbursed 141,087 subloans below US$1,000 with an small average loan size of US$254, reflecting how the demand of credit for productive purposes behave in the localities where the Project was able to reach. </p>

<p>The original target indicators were estimated considering an average subloan size of US$5,000 (the maximum amount set for subloans under the Project was US$50,000). It was also estimated that about 55 percent of final borrowers would access to at least one additional subloan with project funds, and 60 percent of those final borrowers would access to microfinance subloans (less than $1,000). During project implementation, the average loan size was US$1,850.</p>

<p>Moreover, FND kept providing subloans to PFIs under the Project criteria (in a total amount of US$254.5 until December 2020) with the expectation of submitting a reimbursement request of the remaining loan amount (US$79.4 million) as well as of the additional financing (from 2021 and onwards) in case FND would have decided to continue using IBRD funds. FND provided with own funds 150,043 subloans for productive purposes to 123,992 final borrowers in rural areas with an average loan size of US$1,696.</p>

A line of credit is classified "microfinance" if supporting subloans: a) Have an average outstanding balance (gross loan portfolio ÷ number of active borrowers) < 300% of the latest per capita GNI, OR b) Less than $1,000. EITHER circumstance triggers classification as microfinance. Lines of credit and other funding for retail SME sub-loans by Participating Financial Institutions or Community-Managed Loan Funds. Report the cumulative amounts disbursed as of most recent date available. If a split by micro and SME is not available or possible, please use 50% for each as proxy.

title.narrative: Volume of Bank Support: Lines of Credit - SME (cumulative), US$ million
Volume of Bank Support: Lines of Credit - SME (cumulative), US$ million

comment.narrative:
<p>During project preparation, to define the original target, an estimate between volume of micro and SME lines of credit was not available for this core indicator, therefore, the team used a 50 percent split for each one as proxy, following the guidelines. In March 2019, this indicator was adjusted as part of the approval process of the additional financing to reflect i) the current progress; ii) the additional financing; and, iii) the new closing date. In December 2020, the indicator was revised to adjust the dates and targets considering the withdrawn additional financing. Also, the original dates of the Project were reestablished and the split by microfinance and SME targets were included based on the first years of Project implementation.</p>
<p>The Project disbursed US$280.19 million for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), achieving 94 percent of the finally revised target. Under the Project, FND channeled 32,894 subloans to 22,449 SMEs (above US$1,000) with an average size loan of US$8,518 and an average long term of 14 months. </p>

title.narrative: Volume of total loans disbursed under project (cumulative), US$ million
Volume of total loans disbursed under project (cumulative), US$ million

comment.narrative:
<p>The target of this indicator was partially achieved. </p>

<p>The volume of total subloans disbursed with Project funds was US$ 321.72 million, 86 percent of the original target. The target of this indicator was partially achieved because FND decided to not document subloans disbursed in the last 18 months of implementation against the IBRD loan in order to use their own resources as a strategy to optimize the levels of liquidity available in the institution. </p>

<p>FND using their own funds, disbursed US$254,48 million applying the same eligibility criteria defined for this Project. Considering both sources of financing, IBRD loan and FND resources, the total volume of subloans disbursed in the rural economy by FND underthe Project criteria was US$576.2 million. </p>

<p>In addition, as part of the on-lending process, PFIs are required to finance with their own funds at least 20 percent of the approved subloans. From US$322 million disbursed with IBRD loan proceeds the PFIs financed about US$80 million. Likewise, from the US$ 254 million disbursed with FND own funds, the PFIs finance about US$ 63 million (US$143 million from PFIs funds). In total, US$719 million of subloans for productive purposes was disbursed in rural areas. </p>

comment.narrative: <p>During the Project implementation, a total of 10,457 credit lines were given to PFIs, out of which, 494 targeted to microfinanceunits and 9,963 targeted rural small and medium size economic units. The NPLs rate granted to these PFIs, fluctuated between 0 to 4.3 percent from 2016 to 2019. In 2020, 1,767 credit lines that FND  were active, from those, 102 were overdue for more than 90 days due to the economic impact generated by the pandemic lockdown and related restrictions, the NPLs of those lines reached 5.46 percent.</p>

Number of PFIs that receive capacity building from FND

comment.narrative:
<p>This indicator was revised to clarify its definition and to adjust the projected annual targets accordingly. The revised indicator measured unique PFIs (counted only once). </p>

<p>The total number PFIs that received support were 254 (52 percent “dispersoras” and 38 percent SOFOMES), 85 percent of the final target. These PFIs received 478 "apoyos"  to increase their capacity valued at MXN 85,403,418.29 (about US$4.1 million), In 2019 and 2020, FND experienced a reduction in the annual budget of the program in about US$1 million, which limited FND's ability to reach that remaining 15 percent of PFIs.</p>

<p> </p>
